en: The Philippine Department of Health scientifically validates lagundi, a traditional herbal plant, as an effective and safe cough relief for children.
To prevent hand injuries during New Year celebrations, the Philippine government bans dangerous firecrackers like boga and promotes safe alternatives like torches.
The sampaguita, our national flower, releases a sweet fragrance at night to attract pollinating moths, teaching us about plant reproduction and ecology.
National hero Jose Rizal practiced ophthalmology, using his medical science skills to cure his mother’s cataracts and help other visually impaired Filipinos.
The ancient Ifugao rice terraces use a complex stone-walled irrigation system called muyong to prevent soil erosion and safely distribute water for farming.
Under the Universal Health Care Act, the Philippine government guarantees free medical check-ups and vaccinations for all children in public health centers.
Filipino scientist Dr. Fe del Mundo invented a bamboo incubator to keep premature babies warm in rural areas without electricity, saving many infant lives.
The Filipino value of bayanihan is practically applied during typhoons when neighbors safely evacuate together and share relief goods in evacuation centers.
Knowing local health terms like lagnat for fever and pagtatae for diarrhea helps children accurately report symptoms to doctors for faster medical treatment.
The carabao, our national animal, cools its body by wallowing in mud because it lacks sweat glands, teaching us about animal thermoregulation.
Following the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, segregating biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste at home prevents the spread of dengue-carrying mosquitoes in our communities.
During local food festivals, keeping traditional delicacies like kakanin covered with banana leaves protects them from flies and prevents foodborne illnesses among consumers.
